lesson.title: Arccos: The Other Side of Arcsin
lesson.summary: The derivative of arccos x turns out to be the negative twin of the derivative of arcsin x, a fact that falls straight out of the identity arccos x equals pi over 2 minus arcsin x.
lesson.body:
Just as arcsin x was built by restricting sine to the interval where it is one to one, arccos x is built by restricting cosine. Define y = arccos x to be the angle in [0, pi] whose cosine is x. On that interval cosine decreases steadily from 1 down to -1, so every value of x in [-1, 1] corresponds to exactly one angle y, and the inverse function is well defined.

There are two clean ways to find its derivative, and both are worth knowing. The fast route uses the identity arccos x = pi/2 - arcsin x, which holds because sine and cosine are cofunctions of complementary angles. Differentiating both sides, the constant pi/2 drops out, leaving d/dx[arccos x] = -d/dx[arcsin x] = -1/sqrt(1-x^2), using the arcsin derivative from the previous chapter directly.

The from scratch route confirms the same answer and shows why the minus sign has to be there. Let y = arccos x, so cos y = x with y restricted to [0, pi]. Differentiating implicitly gives -sin y times y' = 1, so y' = -1/sin y. Since y lies in [0, pi], sin y is never negative, so sin y = sqrt(1-cos^2 y) = sqrt(1-x^2) using the positive root only. Substituting back gives d/dx[arccos x] = -1/sqrt(1-x^2). The negative sign matches the picture: arccos is a strictly decreasing function on (-1,1), so its slope has to be negative everywhere in that interval.

For practice, differentiate y = arccos(x/2). With u = x/2 and u' = 1/2, the chain rule gives dy/dx = -u'/sqrt(1-u^2) = -(1/2)/sqrt(1 - x^2/4). Since sqrt(1 - x^2/4) = sqrt(4-x^2)/2, this simplifies to dy/dx = -(1/2) divided by (sqrt(4-x^2)/2) = -1/sqrt(4-x^2), valid for -2 < x < 2. At x = 0, the slope is -1/sqrt(4) = -1/2, which matches the graph: arccos(0) = pi/2, right in the middle of the curve where it is falling at a moderate, finite rate.
